title: Benchmark AI on the Task Before You Trust the Workflow
subtitle: Test a small representative sample before turning assistance into a process
description: AI performance is uneven across tasks that can look similarly difficult. Before redesigning a workflow around a model, run it on representative cases, score the outputs against a human-defined standard, and identify where human review is still mandatory.

lifeOsSource.hack: Before adopting AI for a recurring task, test representative cases against a human-defined acceptance standard and record the failure modes.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose a small sample containing easy, ordinary, and awkward cases. Define what counts as acceptable before running the model. Compare AI output with the source or a trusted human result, record failure patterns, and decide which cases can be assisted, which need review, and which should stay human-first.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Do I know the cases where AI is reliable enough to help and the cases where its polished answer should not be trusted?
lifeOsSource.reference: Dell'Acqua et al. — Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier

faq.question: Why test the task instead of judging the model in general?
faq.answer: Because performance can change sharply between tasks that look similar. A model that is useful for one step in a workflow may be unreliable on the next step.

faq.question: What should I score?
faq.answer: Use criteria tied to the real task: factual correctness, completeness, required format, safety, policy compliance, calculation accuracy, or another observable acceptance condition.

intro.html: The useful question is rarely “Is this model smart?” It is “Does this model help on this exact step, with these inputs, under these failure costs?” The difference saves a great deal of automation theatre.

sections.title: 1. Build a representative sample
sections.html: Include ordinary cases and the awkward cases that usually create rework. If you test only clean examples, you learn how the demo behaves, not how the workflow behaves.

sections.title: 2. Define acceptance before seeing output
sections.html: Write the criteria first. Otherwise a fluent answer can quietly lower the standard after the fact.

sections.title: 3. Compare and classify failures
sections.html: Mark errors by type: missing fact, invented fact, wrong calculation, bad judgment, format drift, privacy problem, or another failure that matters in your context.

sections.title: 4. Route work by risk
sections.html: Use the result to separate safe assistance from mandatory review and human-only cases. Re-test after major model, prompt, data, or workflow changes.

references.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
references.claim_scope: In a field experiment with 758 consultants, AI improved performance on tasks inside the tested capability frontier while performance could deteriorate on a task outside it. The finding supports task-level evaluation rather than a blanket assumption that AI helps every adjacent task.

editorialCuration.reason: Make the jagged-frontier result executable as a low-risk workflow evaluation protocol rather than a generic claim about AI productivity.
